w: A pentagonal star fort on the harbor mouth, built in 1798 and battered all night by the Royal Navy in September 1814. It held, and the sight of its oversized garrison flag still flying at dawn inspired Francis Scott Key's poem that became "The Star-Spangled Banner." Now a national monument and historic shrine.
s: The fort that gave America its anthem
_facts: Built 1798, pentagonal bastion fort
Withstood British bombardment Sept 13-14 1814
Flag's survival inspired Key's poem, later the national anthem
National Monument (1925) and Historic Shrine (1939)

w: Founded in 1934 on the collection of William Walters and his son Henry, who began buying art in Paris as a Confederate exile during the Civil War and never really stopped. The Mount Vernon museum now holds work spanning millennia - and true to the founders' wishes, admission has always been free.
s: Free art museum built on two men's obsessions
_facts: Founded/opened 1934
Collection amassed by William T. Walters and son Henry Walters
William Walters collected from Paris as a Confederate loyalist from 1861
Admission is free

w: A sprawling 1,216-acre stream-valley park set aside to protect Baltimore's watersheds from overdevelopment - and, less officially, notorious as a dumping ground: more than 75 bodies have turned up here since the 1940s. By day it hosts the Baltimore Herb Festival and quiet trails; by reputation, something darker.
s: 1,216 acres of woods with a body count
_facts: 1,216 acres, envisioned as a stream-valley park to protect Baltimore's watersheds
Over 75 bodies discovered since the 1940s
Hosts the Baltimore Herb Festival
Part of the Baltimore National Heritage Area

w: Laid out in 1763 on the harbor's north shore, this shipbuilding quarter took in generation after generation of arrivals - Irish, German, Polish, Ukrainian, Latino - and kept its rowhouses and markethouse through it all. Baltimore's oldest waterfront neighborhood, now stitched with antique shops and 120-plus pubs.
_facts: Established c.1763 on the north shore of Baltimore Harbor
Maritime shipbuilding history
Hosted Irish, German, Jewish, Polish, Ukrainian, Latino immigrant communities
Over 120 pubs; one of the first registered historic districts in the US

w: Dedicated in 1839 on a merchant's former country estate, Green Mount helped kick off America's "rural cemetery movement" - part public-health response to overcrowded churchyards, part Romantic-era shrine to nature. Its Gothic Revival gateway and chapel still shelter sculpture by major 19th-century names.
s: A rural cemetery built to escape the churchyard
_facts: Dedicated 1839 on Robert Oliver's former country estate
Baltimore's first rural cemetery, part of the wider rural cemetery movement
Gothic Revival gateway by Robert Cary Long Jr., chapel by Niernsee and Neilson
Listed on National Register of Historic Places 1980

w: Raised in under six months, this red-brick shot tower hit 234 feet in 1828 and briefly stood as the tallest structure in the country - a factory for dropping molten lead through screens to make ammunition. It's the last of four shot towers that once worked Baltimore, and gave its name to the Bullets, now the Wizards.
s: Built in six months, once the tallest in the US
_facts: Completed 1828, 234.25 feet tall, built in under 6 months
Tallest structure in the US when finished
Only surviving shot tower of four in Baltimore
National Historic Landmark 1971; namesake of the Baltimore Bullets basketball team

w: Dedicated in 1959 to replace the old Basilica of the Assumption as the Archdiocese of Baltimore's seat, this Homeland cathedral was built to hold 1,900 worshippers - a mid-century vote of confidence from a diocese with roots in the country's first Catholic bishopric.
_facts: Dedicated 1959
Seat of the Archbishop of Baltimore
Replaced the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Assumption, now co-cathedral
Seats 1,900 people; located in the Homeland area

w: Opened in 1860 under Mayor Thomas Swann, this 745-acre park ranks among the oldest landscaped public parks in the country, alongside Central Park and Philadelphia's Fairmount Park. Reservoirs, woods, and the Maryland Zoo now fill grounds once shaped by some of the era's most sought-after park architects.
s: One of America's oldest landscaped city parks
_facts: 745 acres, opened 1860 under Mayor Thomas Swann
Ranks with Central Park (1858), Fairmount Park (1812), Golden Gate Park as one of the oldest US landscaped parks
Bounded by Druid Park Drive, Swann Drive, Reisterstown Road, JFX/I-83
Contains the Maryland Zoo

w: Isaac Emerson made his fortune selling Bromo-Seltzer for headaches, then spent some of it on this 1911 clock tower styled after Florence's Palazzo Vecchio. It was Baltimore's tallest building for over a decade; the drug factory around it is long gone, but the tower still stands, now backed by a city fire station.
s: A headache remedy that built a 15-story tower
_facts: Built 1907-1911, 289 ft, 15 stories
Built for Isaac Edward Emerson, inventor of Bromo-Seltzer
Tallest building in Baltimore 1911-1923
Original Emerson Drug Co. building razed, replaced by a fire station

n: Edgar Allan Poe House and Museum
w: A small, unassuming rowhouse on North Amity Street where Edgar Allan Poe lived in the 1830s, before the fame that made him famous. Opened as a museum in 1949 and named a National Historic Landmark in 1972, it closed in 2012 over funding, then reopened under a new nonprofit, keeper of the annual Poe Festival.
s: The rowhouse Poe called home in the 1830s
_facts: 203 North Amity Street
Poe's home in the 1830s
Opened as a museum 1949, National Historic Landmark 1972
Closed 2012 over funding, reopened 2013 under Poe Baltimore; hosts the Poe Festival

w: Laid out in 1827 in southeast Baltimore, this park carries Civil War-era battle sites alongside a lake, a swimming pool, and an ice rink - the kind of everything-park that earns nicknames. Locals call it the "Best Backyard in Baltimore," and at 137 acres it's not even the city's biggest, just its friendliest.
_facts: Established 1827, 137 acres
Named for William Patterson
Contains historic battle sites, a lake, pool, ice rink, playgrounds
Nicknamed "Best Backyard in Baltimore"

w: Perched on Federal Hill's harbor edge, on land once fouled by a paint factory and whiskey warehouse, this museum was built for art made outside the academy - by, in its own words, "farmers, housewives, mechanics, the disabled, the homeless." Congress named it America's national museum for visionary art.
s: Congress's official home for outsider art
_facts: Located at 800 Key Highway, Federal Hill
Site was former copper paint factory and whiskey warehouse land
Designated by Congress as America's national museum for visionary/outsider art
No staff curators; uses guest curators; ~4,000-piece permanent collection

w: Rembrandt Peale opened this in 1814 as the first building in the Western Hemisphere designed and built specifically as a museum. It later served as Baltimore's City Hall, then as one of the city's first schools for African-American students, before reopening as a museum in 2022 after a five-year renovation.
_facts: Rembrandt Peale's museum opened 1814, first Western Hemisphere building designed as a museum
Later served as Baltimore's City Hall 1830-1875 and 1878-1887
Housed one of the first schools for African-American students in Baltimore
Reopened 2022 after 5-year renovation

w: A small museum tucked into Fell's Point that keeps the record of Baltimore's Slavic immigrant story - Polish, Ukrainian, Czech, Croatian, Serbian, and more, folded into one storefront collection. A quiet counterpoint to the harbor crowds, telling the side of the neighborhood the tour boats skip.
s: Fell's Point's shrine to Baltimore's Slavic wave
_facts: Located in Fell's Point, Baltimore
Dedicated to Polish and Slavic heritage of Baltimore
Covers Belarusian, Bulgarian, Carpatho-Rusyn, Croatian, Czech, Lemko, Moravian, Russian, Serbian, Slovak, Slovene, Ukrainian heritage

w: Finished in 1829 for the brand-new Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, this stone arch over the Gwynns Falls is the country's first stone masonry railroad bridge - and the oldest one still in service. Named for Charles Carroll of Carrollton, last surviving signer of the Declaration of Independence, it now carries CSX freight.
s: America's oldest railroad bridge, still working
_facts: Built 1828-1829 for the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad
First stone masonry railroad bridge in the US, oldest still in service
Named for Charles Carroll of Carrollton
National Historic Landmark 1971; now owned/operated by CSX Transportation

w: Baltimore's tight-knit Italian-American quarter has spent generations keeping its rowhouses in the family rather than selling them on, which is partly why the enclave still feels so intact. Every summer it projects movies onto a wall at High and Stiles Streets, a film festival now as traditional as the restaurants.
s: An Italian-American enclave that keeps to itself
_facts: Southeastern Baltimore neighborhood with strong Italian-American heritage
Longstanding tradition of keeping houses within the family
Annual outdoor film festival projected onto a wall at High and Stiles Streets

w: Sponsored by the city and a wartime Committee of Vigilance after the 1814 Battle of Baltimore, this monument sits squarely in the middle of Calvert Street between two courthouses - honoring the militia who held off the British fleet at Fort McHenry and the stand on Hampstead Hill.
s: A War of 1812 memorial planted in the street
_facts: Commemorates the Battle of Baltimore, War of 1812
Sponsored by the city and the Committee of Vigilance and Safety, led by Mayor Edward Johnson
Sits in the middle of North Calvert Street between two courthouses
Honors those who died in September 1814
